lead: A two-way finite automaton is a DFA whose read head may step left as well as right. The input sits on a tape with a left end marker ⊢ and a right end marker ⊣, so the head cannot fall off the ends. The extra freedom feels powerful, yet it buys nothing: two-way and one-way machines accept exactly the same languages, the regular ones. The proof idea, the crossing sequence, survives in space-bounded complexity and in streaming lower bounds. Only a few universities teach the topic.
prereq: You need: DFA (1.2), NFA (1.4) and the transition notation of 1.3.

sections.h3: The machine, the tape and the markers

blocks.text: A two-way finite automaton is the tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F): Q is a finite set of states, Σ the input alphabet, q₀ the start state, F ⊆ Q the final states. The new part is the transition function δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {⊢, ⊣}) → Q × {L, R}. It takes a state and a tape symbol and returns a next state plus a direction, L for one cell left, R for one cell right. The function may be partial: when δ is undefined for the current state and tape symbol, the machine halts. For a nondeterministic 2FA the transition function becomes a relation, δ ⊆ Q × (Σ ∪ {⊢, ⊣}) × Q × {L, R}, so several moves may be possible from one configuration; the machine accepts if some run halts in F.

The input string of length n occupies cells 1 to n of a tape. Cell 0 holds the left end marker ⊢, cell n+1 the right end marker ⊣. The markers are not in Σ. The head starts on ⊢. A legal 2FA never moves left from ⊢ or right from ⊣; if δ is undefined for the current state and marker, the run halts. Unlike a DFA, a 2FA may read the same cell many times, so it keeps no count of input consumed.

A configuration is a state together with a head position. The machine accepts when a run halts in a state of F. A deterministic 2FA may also loop forever on some input; a loop is neither acceptance nor rejection.

sections.h3: Why two-way movement adds no power

blocks.text: Theorem. Deterministic two-way FAs, nondeterministic two-way FAs and ordinary DFAs accept exactly the same class: the regular languages. Every DFA is a 2FA that never moves left, so one direction is free. The other direction is the surprise: every 2FA can be simulated by a DFA.

The reason is the crossing sequence. Cut the tape between two cells and watch the head cross that cut. The crossing sequence is the ordered list of states in which the head crosses, left to right or right to left. For a fixed machine only finitely many such lists exist. A DFA can remember, cut by cut, which lists are possible, and that finite record decides acceptance.

The simulating DFA can be exponentially larger than the 2FA: an n-state 2FA may need a DFA with exponentially many states (roughly 2<sup>cn</sup> for some constant c). That blow-up is why the proof is skipped in this unit.

figure.caption: The head runs right through q1, and the end marker sends it one step left into q2. That single backward move is what an ordinary DFA cannot do.

spec.aria: Five circles; the head runs right along q1 until the end marker sends it one step left to q2, which accepts on a and falls into the dead state on b.

examples.question: Using the machine in the figure (states q0, q1, q2, qf, d), trace the inputs aba and abb on the tape, give the state and head position after each move, and state the accepted language. The input alphabet is {a, b}.
steps: aba. Tape ⊢ a b a ⊣. δ(q0, ⊢) = (q1, R): the head moves to cell 1, holding a.
q1 loops on a and b with R. The head crosses a, b, a and lands on ⊣, still in q1.
δ(q1, ⊣) = (q2, L): the head steps back onto the last symbol a.
δ(q2, a) = (qf, R). qf ∈ F, so aba is accepted.
abb. Tape ⊢ a b b ⊣. The same run reaches q2 with the head on the last symbol, now b.
δ(q2, b) = (d, R), and d ∉ F. abb is rejected.
Only the last cell matters, so L = { w ∈ {a, b}⁺ : w ends in a }. The empty input ⊢ ⊣ leaves the head in q2 on ⊢, a non-final halt, so it is rejected too.
examples.answer: aba is accepted into qf, abb is rejected into d, and the machine accepts exactly the non-empty strings over {a, b} that end in a.

traps: Two-way movement adds no power. Writing that a 2FA accepts aⁿbⁿ is the classic wrong answer.
Two-way is not two-tape. One tape, one head; only the direction is free.
δ may be partial. If the head is on ⊢ or ⊣ in a state with no move, the run halts there; a legal machine either has the move or halts and never walks off the tape.
The equivalent DFA exists but may be exponentially larger, so no small DFA is promised.
A deterministic 2FA can loop. Not rejected yet is not accepted; acceptance needs halting in F.

quiz.q: What does the transition function of a 2FA return?
quiz.a: A next state and a direction, L or R.

quiz.q: Why does the tape carry ⊢ and ⊣?
quiz.a: As end markers, so the head cannot leave the tape.

quiz.q: Why does a two-way head add no power?
quiz.a: Every 2FA has an equivalent DFA, so the accepted class stays regular.

quiz.q: Trace input ba on the figure's machine and give the verdict.
quiz.a: q0 reads ⊢ and moves R to q1; q1 reads b, then a, moving R each time; reads ⊣ and moves L to q2 on a; q2 reads a and goes to qf. Accept, since ba ends in a.

quiz.q: Bound the moves of a halting 2FA run on input length n, with |Q| states.
quiz.a: There are |Q|(n+2) configurations. A halting run repeats none, so it makes at most |Q|(n+2) moves, linear in n.

quiz.q: Why may the equivalent DFA be exponentially larger?
quiz.a: It tracks the possible crossing sequences at every cut, and there are exponentially many of them.

beyond: Not for the exam. Crossing sequences are the standard tool in space-bounded complexity, where a machine also sweeps its head both ways over the input. They also give lower bounds in streaming, where one pass must do what no small two-way machine can. Search for 'two-way finite automaton' and 'crossing sequence' to go further.
